paras: The lynching of Sidney King was the hanging of a Black youth by local residents in Hernando County, Florida, in late June or early July 1881. King was accused of shooting and cutting the three children of Sheriff J. Bart Mickler and robbing the sheriff's house, and he was hanged before a crowd reported as 200 citizens. A Jacksonville dispatch carried the story across the country, and papers in the South and North treated the hanging as deserved punishment.

According to the Jacksonville dispatch, Sheriff Mickler lived some miles from the Hernando County court house and, having to go there on 29 June, left his children, aged eight, eleven and fourteen, alone with "a negro named King, to whom he had been very kind." The Savannah Morning News gave his name as Sidney King, "a negro boy, seventeen years of age," whom the sheriff had "rescued from the clutches of the law."

The dispatch said King shot and mortally wounded the oldest child, drove the other two into the woods, shot one dead and cut the throat of the youngest, then robbed the house and lay in wait for the sheriff. A neighbor accompanied Mickler home, and King's alleged plan was thwarted; the Chicago Tribune wrote that he "was made prisoner." The Lake City Reporter told it differently, saying the children had caught a man stealing their father's money on Tuesday night and that he shot all three to hide his guilt.

King was reported to have confessed, after which he "was hanged in the presence of and with the approbation of two hundred citizens," a crowd that the Memphis and New York copies described as "white and colored." The Chicago Tribune said simply that "the people in the vicinity lynched him," and the Savannah Morning News that "a whole community" pursued, captured and executed him. None of the reports gives the place or the day of the hanging.

No report of an inquest or of any action against the lynchers appears in the coverage. Florida papers followed the children: on 26 July the Weekly Floridian reported that Bloxham, the youngest, was recovering from knife wounds, but on 10 August the Savannah Morning News reported that he had died after surviving his injuries for a month.

The Jacksonville dispatch appeared on 6 July under headlines such as "THE FATE OF A FIEND" in Savannah, "A TERRIBLE CRIME" in Memphis, "TRIPLE MURDER AND LYNCHING" in New York and "Judge Lynch" in Augusta, Maine. Its language called King a "fiend" and "brute" and said he "died sullen and unrepenting," while digests in Wisconsin and Kentucky papers the following week cut it to a few lines ending with the lynching. Some digests garbled the details, printing the sheriff's name as Micken, Mackler or Nickler and, in Watertown, placing Hernando County in Mississippi.

Editorial comment accepted the lynching: the Chicago Tribune wrote that the murderer "has already paid the penalty of his crime," and the Savannah Morning News, while saying mob law "is to be condemned in the strongest terms," called it "little wonder" that the community acted. Because the collection of Black newspapers begins in 1900, no Black-press account of the lynching is available.

Reports disagreed about the children: the dispatch called it a triple murder, the Lake City Reporter said one child died at once and two were alive on Thursday, and the later Florida items show that the youngest lived about a month. Copies of the same dispatch also differed on whether the wounded children were "able" or "unable" to describe the attack.

reader.title: Lynching of Sidney King
bases: A Black man accused of killing a sheriff's children was captured and hanged by local people before a crowd of 200 (A2, A5, A4).

The wire says King was captured, confessed and was hanged before and with the approval of 200 citizens, the Chicago Tribune that 'the people in the vicinity lynched him', and the Savannah Morning News that a 'whole community' captured and executed him under 'mob law' as punishment for the alleged murders (A2, A5, A4).

The Jacksonville wire (A2, A8), a Savannah editorial with details not in the wire (King's name and age, A4) and the Chicago Tribune's own paragraph (A5) agree that King was captured and lynched, and the Lake City Reporter had him caught and likely to be lynched (A3).

accounts.label: Jacksonville wire
accounts.gist: King shot and cut the three children, robbed the house and lay in wait for the sheriff, was thwarted, captured, confessed and was hanged before and with the approval of 200 citizens; he 'died sullen and unrepenting'.

accounts.label: Lake City Reporter (via Savannah)
accounts.gist: The children caught a negro stealing their father's money on Tuesday night; he shot all three and cut one's throat; the negro had been caught and would 'probably be lynched'.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News editorial
accounts.gist: Named the accused as Sidney King, 17, whom the sheriff had rescued 'from the clutches of the law'; a whole community pursued, captured and executed him.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News said mob law 'is to be condemned' but that it was 'little wonder' a community executed King, and headlined the wire 'THE FATE OF A FIEND' with 'The Miscreant Promptly Lynched'.
The Chicago Tribune wrote that 'The murderer has already paid the penalty of his crime' and Memphis headlined it 'A TERRIBLE CRIME'.
Northern and Midwestern papers ran the wire or a short digest in news columns without comment.

versions.value: Oldest mortally wounded, one shot dead, youngest throat cut; one and perhaps both wounded now dead
One died at once; two alive Thursday morning
One child survived long enough to tell the father
Youngest, Bloxham, recovering (26 July); died after surviving a month (10 August)

conflicts.note: The later Florida items (A23, A24) are the best evidence on the children's fates; the wire's 'triple murder' was written before outcomes were known.
Variant copies of the same wire.
The wire dates the sheriff's trip to the court house, not necessarily the hour of the attack.
The Watertown digest's 'Miss.' is an error; all other copies say Florida.
